elements.element: New York law governs the Agreement.
elements.evidence: 28.1 is retained verbatim: "This Agreement and each dispute arising from it are governed by the laws of the State of New York, without regard to conflict-of-law principles." No arbitration clause appears anywhere in the Agreement, so nothing displaces the New York choice of law.

elements.element: State and federal courts in New York County have exclusive jurisdiction.
elements.evidence: Rendered 28.2 states "The state and federal courts located in New York County, New York have exclusive jurisdiction, and each Party irrevocably submits to personal jurisdiction and waives any objection based on venue or inconvenient forum." The prior second sentence permitting a Party to seek temporary injunctive relief "in another court with jurisdiction" is deleted, so no another-court carve-out survives to undercut exclusivity.

elements.element: The governing law is Delaware, California, or England and Wales.
elements.evidence: 28.1 selects New York law only; no Delaware, California, or England and Wales law is chosen. This is expected because the proposal targets the preferred level, which is fully met.

elements.element: The dispute forum is the corresponding Delaware or California courts, or the courts of London for England and Wales law.
elements.evidence: 28.2 designates the state and federal courts in New York County, not Delaware/California courts or the courts of London. Inapplicable given the preferred level is achieved.

reasons: Preferred level is position-complete on the operative rendered text: New York law in 28.1 is untouched and 28.2 now states unqualified exclusive jurisdiction in the state and federal courts of New York County, with the another-court injunctive-relief carve-out removed.
Fallback level is not met (and need not be): no Delaware, California, or England and Wales law or corresponding forum is selected. A single complete level suffices for position-completeness.

Minimality holds: the edit is confined to deleting the one sentence that defeated the exclusivity element. The CISG exclusion in 28.1, the personal-jurisdiction submission and forum-inconvenience waiver in 28.2, and the 28.3 pre-filing process are all retained; no survival tail, expense language, procedure, or other extra requirement was added, and no favourable wording outside the two preferred elements was touched.

Intent is preserved: the choice-of-law sentence, CISG exclusion, mutual submission language, and pre-filing dispute mechanics survive without contradiction, and the deletion leaves no undefined term or dangling cross-reference (28.2 reads as a complete sentence on its own).

Note for the drafter, not a defect against the checklist: the deleted carve-out was mutual and gave us as well as Vendor an emergency-relief avenue in the court where confidential information or IP is at risk. If preserving that practical remedy matters commercially, the alternative is to accept 28.2 as originally drafted at the preferred position and note the carve-out in the rationale rather than redline it; as rendered, the exclusivity element is unambiguously met.

Severity is narrow in substance: the underlying clause already sat at the preferred jurisdiction and venue, and the only gap was the exclusivity carve-out, so this is a low-impact repair rather than a material fallback failure.
